issues.legal_issue: A market-value assessment based on the land’s development and its potential for building use is not vitiated by an error of principle.
material_facts: The acquired land was in a developed area and near developed localities belonging to private parties and the Government.
The High Court found that the land had potential for building use and assessed its market value on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the market-value determination, finding no error of principle in the High Court’s assessment.
issues.legal_principle: In determining market value, the land’s location in a developed area, proximity to developed localities, and potential for building use are relevant considerations. The Court relied on no earlier case or statutory provision in deciding this issue.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and (land_in_developed_area and near_developed_localities and building_use_potential)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding concerns an appeal about compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.land_in_developed_area: The acquired land was situated in an area that was developed.
predicates.near_developed_localities: The acquired land was near developed localities.
predicates.building_use_potential: The acquired land had potential for use for building purposes.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compensation for acquired land that is in a developed area, near developed localities, and has building-use potential, the market-value determination is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The applicable amendment entitles claimants to the enhanced statutory solatium and interest when the reference court’s award was made before the amendment.
material_facts: The reference court made its award on November 2, 1973.
The High Court applied Amendment Act 68 of 1984 and awarded enhanced solatium, interest, and an additional amount.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the amendment applied and that the claimants were entitled to solatium at 15% and interest at 6% on the enhanced compensation from the date possession was taken until the amount was deposited in court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Amendment Act 68 of 1984, holding that it applied in view of the date of the reference court’s award. It relied on no earlier case in deciding this issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.reference_court_award_precedes_amendment: The reference court made its compensation award before the relevant amendment applied.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition compensation proceeding has a reference-court award made before the relevant amendment applied, the claimants receive the enhanced statutory compensation benefits.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land held under a continuing long-term tenancy may be apportioned between tenant and landlord by considering the duration and nature of the tenancy rights and the tenant’s improvements.
material_facts: The tenant received a lease in 1949 for 30 years, with a right to renew from time to time up to a maximum of 99 years.
The tenancy was terminated in 1960, but the termination was challenged successfully; the tenant remained in possession.
The government initiated acquisition under the land-acquisition law in 1967, while the tenant remained in possession, and the land had not been taken following the attempted termination.
The tenant had enjoyed part of the 99-year lease for 18 years when the land was acquired.
The High Court apportioned compensation 75% to the tenant and 25% to the landlord; the government challenged that apportionment.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that an apportionment of 60% to the tenant and 40% to the landlord was reasonable and directed payment on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The apportionment must account for relevant factors, including the lease’s duration, the nature of the tenant’s right to enjoy the leasehold interest, and improvements made by the tenant. A tenant whose tenancy remains in force when the government chooses to acquire the land may be entitled to compensation for the tenancy right. If the government owns the land and instead terminates the lease under its covenants and takes possession before acquisition, the tenant may have no right to compensation. The Court considered Mangat Ram v. State of Haryana, [1996] 8 SCC 664, and Inder Parshad v. Union of India, [1994] 5 SCC 239, which upheld 75%/25% apportionments in their circumstances, and distinguished Col. Sir Harinder Singh Brar Bans Bahadur v. Bihari Lal, [1994] 4 SCC 523, where the tenant’s statutory right to the entire land entitled the tenant to all compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_dispute: The proceeding concerns the division of compensation for land acquired by the government between a tenant and a landlord.
predicates.tenant_in_possession_when_acquisition_be: The tenant remained in possession when the government began acquiring the land.
predicates.tenancy_continued_after_termination_was_: The attempted termination of the tenancy was successfully challenged, and the tenancy remained in effect.
predicates.long_term_lease_partly_enjoyed: The tenant held a long-term lease and had enjoyed only part of its term when the land was acquired.

issues.definition: When acquired land is subject to a partly enjoyed long-term tenancy that continued after a challenged termination and the tenant remained in possession when acquisition began, compensation is apportioned sixty to the tenant and forty to the landlord.
